title: Raspberry Pi Controller
description: First embeded system-ish project with a Raspberry Pi5, ESP32, and 433MHz transmitter/receivers to create a universal remote to control things like lights remotely

elements.content: The *"Problem"*

Here's the *"problem":* All the lights in my room are controlled by basic 433 MHz remotes. Having to keep track of multiple remotes is a pain, like coming home at night and having no idea where your remote is.
So here's the solution: A device that can record any 433 MHz remote and that can be accessed remotely to control smart devices from any device, anywhere

elements.title: Basic 433 MHz Remote
elements.alt: Image of a 433 MHz remote that controls a lamp that came with said lamp.

elements.content: [433MHz](https://homey.app/en-us/wiki/433-mhz/) is the radio frequency used by many simple commercial applications like garage doors, lights, lamps, smart switches, etc. This project specifically targets 433 MHz only.
Contents
This controller's construction can be broken into these parts:
The Receiver and Transmitter
Many simple devices work by listening for specific packets of binary data on a specific frequency (433 MHz in this case)
Normally this data would be transmitted from a remote that came with the device, but you could also make your own using an RF transmitter/receiver on the same frequency

elements.alt: Picture of a 433MHz superhet receiver and transmitter
elements.title: 433 MHz Transmitter/Receiver

elements.content: The specific RF transmitter/receiver model is a "[Superheterodyne UHF ASK Remote Control Module](https://a.co/d/0ioosRzQ)"
Data and ASK Modulation

A common/simple way to transmit binary data on a frequency is Amplitude Shift Keying (ASK). In ASK, HIGH and LOW amplitudes represent 1s and 0s respectively. An RF receiver can listen to a remote to decode its binary data and save it to be reused.

elements.title: ASK Modulation Diagram
elements.alt: (Credit to GeeksForGeeks.org) Image shows how digital binary sequences are converted to modulated output waves with precise timings

elements.content: Copying Remotes

Below is actually how my lamp remote is stored on my Raspberry Pi. Pulse patterns can be saved in different ways, but this way works by identifying the protocol used, the timings between pulses, and the binary data. These values can be used to reconstruct the ASK pulses and "emulate" the original remote.

{
	"name": "LampON",
	"type": "rc_remote",
	"protocol": 1,
	"delay": 387,
	"bits": 24,
	"value": 7869186
}

Sometimes a protocol can't easily be identified. In these cases, the remote can be stored as raw timings between HIGH and LOW pulses. However, this requires much more data so it won't be shown. Either way, this data can be used to tell the transmitter how to recreate these pulses, effectively becoming the remote.
The ESP32

An ESP32 is a low-cost microcontroller (MCU). MCUs are chips that contain essential computer components like the CPU, RAM, Clock, and I/O on a single chip. The ESP32 is poular because it's fairly cheap and powerful, and even has WiFi and Bluetooth capabilities.

elements.alt: Image of ESP32 sitting on a PCB
elements.title: ESP32 DevKit C4

elements.content: The ESP32 used here is an [ESP32-DevKitC-32E](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B09MQJWQN2?ref=ppx_yo2ov_dt_b_fed_asin_title&th=1), however an ESP32 is not strictly necessary as WiFi/Bluetooth aren't needed.

*So why an ESP32 _and_ Raspberry Pi 5?*   The main reason I used an ESP32 is to precisely control the RF transmitter/receiver. As mentioned above, the RF signals have exact timings on the scale of microseconds. A Raspberry Pi 5 runs a full linux operating system alongside your program. Its resources are so split that it's hard to get exact timings. An MCU like an ESP32, however, runs a single program directly on the chip. This allows is to achieve much better timing precision.
RF Controls
The ESP32 communicates directly with the RF receiver/transmitter for recording and playing remotes. The ESP32 uses UART communication to receive commands and send data to and from the Raspberry Pi.
[UART](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_asynchronous_receiver-transmitter) is a communication protocl that uses two wires, TX (transmit) and RX (receive), to communicate in plaintext.
For example, it might receive a command on its TX pin that looks like:
{"cmd": "playRC", "protocol": 1, "delay": 387, "bits": 24, "value": 7869186}
The ESP32 would then identify the command `"cmd":"playRC"` and play the right RF signal from the given data
